pages.text: The Great Kanak Revolt of 1878 was a major uprising by the Kanak people in New Caledonia. A famous leader of this movement was Ataï, the great chief of Komalé. The Kanak people refer to this historic event as the War of Ataï.
pages.caption: Surrender of the Kanak rebels to Henri Riviére (J. Férat, 1881)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Surrender of the Kanak rebels to Henri Riviére, 1878.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Surrender of the Kanak rebels to Henri Riviére (J. Férat, 1881)

pages.text: France declared New Caledonia a French colony in 1853. The administration used a system of conquest that favored alliances and opposed resistance. European settlers began to arrive, and land was taken from the local people to build public wealth and encourage settlement.

In 1868, the administration made rules requiring indigenous people to live in specific delimited areas called reserves. These rules stated that indigenous property could not be sold or given away, which caused severe land loss and destabilization for the Kanak population.

The discovery of nickel ore in 1870 started a rush of new settlers and immigrants. At the same time, growing livestock numbers caused problems. Cattle strayed into traditional food crops like yams and taro, destroying local gardens and polluting water reserves and sacred sites.

Deep discontent grew among the Melanesians over many years. In 1878, Ataï met with the colonial governor at Teremba. He poured a bag of earth to show what they once had, and then a bag of stones to show what the colonists had left them.

After the conflict, between 1,000 and 1,500 Kanaks were deported to nearby and distant islands. Rebel chiefs were executed without trial during operations, while others faced court-martial. The indigenous population steadily declined in the following decades.

pages.text: The Great Kanak Revolt of 1878 describes the major insurrection of the Kanak people in New Caledonia. The movement was centered around the iconic figure of Ataï, the great chief of Komalé, whom the Kanaks remember in connection with the War of Ataï.

pages.text: Following European discovery in 1774, New Caledonia was frequented by adventurers and traders before France proclaimed it a colony in 1853. The French administration implemented a conquest legislation that favored political alliances and utilized local rivalries. Governor Eugène du Bouzet subsequently declared all unoccupied land to be property of the French government.

To organize the indigenous population, the colonial administration created the legal notion of the tribe in 1867 to enforce collective responsibility. By 1868, authorities required Melanesians to relocate into delimited reserves. These reserves prevented indigenous property from being sold or leased, leading to widespread dispossession.

The discovery of high-concentration nickel ore in 1870 triggered a nickel rush that brought various immigrant groups to the region. Meanwhile, European agriculture and livestock expanded dramatically. Unenclosed cattle strayed across the landscape, destroying traditional food crops such as yams and taro while polluting springs and sacred sites.

Melanesian discontent had been building for years amid growing land dispossessions and conflicts. In 1878, Ataï met with colonial governor Léopold de Pritzbuer at Teremba. In a famous gesture, Ataï poured a bag of earth representing what the Kanaks once held, followed by a bag of stones representing what the colonists had left them.

In the aftermath of the revolt, between 1,000 and 1,500 Kanaks were deported to various islands, including the Île des Pins and Bélep. Most rebel chiefs were executed during military operations without a formal trial, while the indigenous population experienced a significant decline recorded by official censuses.

C1-C2.headline: Causes and Aftermath of the 1878 Revolt

pages.text: The Great Kanak Revolt of 1878 denotes the widespread insurrection staged by the indigenous Kanak population against French colonial rule in New Caledonia. The rebellion is historically anchored by the leadership of Ataï, the great chief of Komalé, and is locally designated as the War of Ataï.
pages.caption: Surrender of the Kanak rebels to Henri Riviére (J. Férat, 1881)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Surrender of the Kanak rebels to Henri Riviére, 1878.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Surrender of the Kanak rebels to Henri Riviére (J. Férat, 1881)

pages.text: Following initial visits by various maritime operators and missionaries, France proclaimed New Caledonia a colony in 1853. The administration established a framework of conquest that exploited inter-tribal dissensions. Through administrative declarations, the colonial government asserted ownership over unoccupied lands, systematically superseding prior customary agreements.

Administrative decrees in 1867 instituted the legal concept of the tribe to enforce collective civic responsibility. By 1868, the administration mandated the confinement of Melanesians within delimited reserves. These designated territories prohibited indigenous property alienation, accelerating structural dispossession and demographic destabilization.

The 1870 discovery of garnierite initiated a significant nickel rush, diversifying the non-Kanak population through foreign immigration. Concurrently, rapid pastoral expansion led to severe environmental degradation. Unenclosed cattle populations destroyed traditional horticultural crops like yams and taro while simultaneously polluting vital water resources and sacred sites.

Decades of systemic land expropriation culminated in open conflict. Prior to the 1878 insurrection, Ataï articulated indigenous grievances to the colonial governor of New Caledonia, Léopold de Pritzbuer, at Teremba. He symbolically presented two bags: one containing earth representing what they had, and another containing stones representing what settlers left them.

The suppression of the revolt resulted in the penal deportation of 1,000 to 1,500 Kanaks to peripheral islands. Captured rebel chiefs were typically executed summarily during operations without judicial proceedings. Official census data from subsequent decades documented a sharp contraction in the indigenous population.

title: History of the Anti-Nuclear Movement
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The anti-nuclear movement is a social group. It works to stop nuclear technology. People in this movement include environmental groups and direct action groups. Some groups only want to stop nuclear weapons. Other groups want to stop both nuclear weapons and nuclear power plants.
pages.caption: Anti-nuclear power plant Rally following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster on 19 September 2011, at Meiji Shrine complex in Tokyo, Japan

evidence.fileTitle: File:Anti-Nuclear Power Plant Rally on 19 September 2011 at Meiji Shrine Outer Garden 03.JPG
evidence.articleCaption: Anti-nuclear power plant Rally following the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster on 19 September 2011, at Meiji Shrine complex in Tokyo, Japan

pages.text: People have talked about nuclear weapons policy for a long time. Scientists and diplomats debated this topic even before the atomic bombings in 1945. Later, many people became worried about nuclear testing. In 1963, many countries agreed to stop testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere.

Opposition to nuclear power started to grow in the 1960s. In the early 1970s, people held large protests against a planned power plant in Germany. The project was cancelled in 1975. This success inspired more protests against nuclear power in Europe and North America.
pages.caption: Anti-nuclear protest near nuclear waste disposal centre at Gorleben in Northern Germany, on 8 November 2008

evidence.articleCaption: Anti-nuclear protest near nuclear waste disposal centre at Gorleben in Northern Germany, on 8 November 2008

pages.text: Many large protests happened over the years. In 1977, thousands of people protested in Spain. In 1982, one million people marched in New York City against nuclear weapons. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, people also marched in Rome to protest the Italian nuclear program.
pages.caption: 169,000 people attended an anti-nuclear protest in Bonn, West Germany, on 14 October 1979, following the Three Mile Island accident.

evidence.articleCaption: 169,000 people attended an anti-nuclear protest in Bonn, West Germany, on 14 October 1979, following the Three Mile Island accident.

pages.text: For many years after the Chernobyl disaster, nuclear power was less popular. Later, some countries started talking about nuclear power again. Then, the 2011 Fukushima accident happened. This new accident brought back strong opposition to nuclear power in many countries around the world.
pages.caption: Following the 2011 Japanese Fukushima nuclear disaster, authorities shut down the nation's 54 nuclear power plants. As of 2013, the Fukushima site remains highly radioactive, with some 160,000 evacuees still living in temporary housing, and some land will be unfarmable for centuries. pages.text: Anti-nuclear groups suggest other ways to get energy. They say people should use energy more carefully. They also support using renewable energy sources like sunlight and wind. These natural energy flows can help reduce our reliance on nuclear power and other fossil fuels.

The anti-nuclear movement is a global social movement that opposes various nuclear technologies. Environmental movements, professional organisations, and direct action groups participate at local, national, and international levels. While the initial objective was nuclear disarmament, opposition expanded since the late 1960s to include nuclear power as well.

pages.text: Scientists and diplomats debated nuclear weapons policy prior to the 1945 atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Public concern regarding nuclear weapons testing grew around 1954 following the Castle Bravo disaster. Consequently, many countries ratified the Partial Test Ban Treaty in 1963, prohibiting atmospheric nuclear testing.

Local opposition to nuclear power emerged in the early 1960s. Large protests arose in the early 1970s against the proposed Wyhl Nuclear Power Plant in southern Germany. The project was cancelled in 1975, and this success inspired similar opposition across Europe and North America. Public protest became a major force during this decade.

pages.text: Massive demonstrations occurred globally over the following decades. In 1979, a protest in New York City drew 200,000 people after the Three Mile Island accident. The largest demonstration took place on June 12, 1982, when one million people protested against nuclear weapons in New York City. Following the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, up to 200,000 people marched in Rome.

The 2011 Fukushima nuclear accident subsequently undermined proposed industry revivals and renewed global opposition, leading several nations to phase out nuclear power entirely.

pages.text: Anti-nuclear groups argue that reliance on nuclear energy can be reduced through energy conservation and efficiency measures. Furthermore, they advocate for transitioning to renewable energy sources. These alternatives involve natural phenomena such as sunlight, wind, tides, plant growth, and geothermal heat to sustainably power society without nuclear risks.

The anti-nuclear movement encompasses a diverse coalition of direct action groups, environmental movements, and professional organizations operating across local, national, and international spheres. Although the foundational objective centered on nuclear disarmament, the scope broadened significantly since the late 1960s to incorporate staunch opposition to commercial nuclear power generation.

Public opposition directly preceded the decommissioning of several prominent nuclear facilities.

title: The History and Protection of World Heritage
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: World Heritage Sites are important places and landmarks. They have legal protection under an international treaty administered by UNESCO. These sites are chosen for their great cultural, historical, or scientific value to humanity. They include ancient ruins, forests, lakes, and monuments.
pages.caption: Site No. 274: Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu in Peru, an example of a mixed (natural and cultural) heritage site

evidence.articleCaption: Site No. 274: Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu in Peru, an example of a mixed (natural and cultural) heritage site

pages.text: The story of these protected places began in Egypt. In 1954, the government decided to build a new dam. The water would cover many cultural treasures of ancient Egypt and Nubia. Egypt and Sudan asked UNESCO for help to rescue the endangered monuments and sites.
pages.caption: UNESCO World Heritage Sites

evidence.articleCaption: UNESCO World Heritage Sites

pages.text: UNESCO launched a campaign to save the monuments. Workers excavated hundreds of sites and moved important temples to higher ground. This successful rescue project led to other safeguarding campaigns around the world and inspired a new international convention to protect cultural heritage.
pages.caption: Site No. 252: Taj Mahal in India, an example of a cultural heritage site

evidence.articleCaption: Site No. 252: Taj Mahal in India, an example of a cultural heritage site

pages.text: Countries must follow a specific process to list a site. First, a country puts a site on a tentative list. Then, experts evaluate the nomination file. The World Heritage Committee meets once a year to decide which properties to add to the official World Heritage List.

Being listed brings international recognition, legal protection, and possible funds for conservation. However, sites can also face dangers like wars, natural disasters, pollution, or mass tourism. UNESCO wants to preserve these irreplaceable treasures so future generations can enjoy them.
pages.caption: The Galápagos Islands (World Heritage Site No. 1) in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of South America, had its boundaries extended in 2001 and 2003, and was included on the danger list from 2007 to 2010.

pages.text: World Heritage Sites are landmarks and areas possessing cultural, historical, or scientific significance. Administered by UNESCO, these sites receive legal protection under an international treaty. They are judged to contain heritage of outstanding value to humanity, ranging from ancient ruins and historical structures to forests, islands, and deserts.

pages.text: The origin of the program dates back to the mid-20th century. In 1954, Egypt planned to build the Aswan High Dam, which threatened to inundate a large stretch of the Nile valley containing ancient treasures. Consequently, the governments of Egypt and Sudan requested UNESCO's assistance in 1959 to rescue the endangered monuments.

pages.text: The Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage was adopted in November 1972. To nominate a site, a country must first include it on a tentative list before submitting a nomination file. Advisory bodies evaluate the files, and the World Heritage Committee makes the final decision.

Listing can significantly increase tourism revenue and provide funds for conservation. Nonetheless, listed properties can face serious threats, including armed conflict, natural disasters, pollution, and rapid visitor growth. Sites facing severe risks may be added to a danger list to encourage counteractive measures and preserve them for future generations.

pages.text: World Heritage Sites comprise internationally protected landmarks and areas recognized for their outstanding cultural, historical, or scientific significance. Governed by a UNESCO-administered treaty, these designations encompass diverse entities, from ancient architectural structures and urban centers to vulnerable wilderness areas and natural landscapes.

pages.text: The international framework originated from a major preservation crisis in Egypt. The planned construction of the Aswan High Dam threatened to submerge extensive Nile valley regions rich in ancient Egyptian and Nubian heritage. In 1959, the governments of Egypt and Sudan requested UNESCO to assist them.

pages.text: Following years of international collaboration, the General Conference of UNESCO adopted the safeguarding convention in November 1972. Nomination procedures require states parties to maintain a tentative list, compile detailed nomination files, and submit to rigorous evaluations by specialized advisory bodies prior to annual committee reviews.

While inscription yields international recognition, legal protection, and potential financial assistance, listed properties frequently encounter vulnerabilities. Adverse pressures such as armed conflict, industrial pollution, and unregulated tourism can precipitate inscription on the List of World Heritage in Danger, thereby mobilizing international awareness and remedial conservation strategies.

pages.text: World Heritage Sites are landmarks and areas possessing cultural, historical, or scientific significance. Administered by UNESCO, these sites receive legal protection under an international treaty. They are judged to contain heritage of outstanding value to humanity, ranging from ancient ruins and historical structures to forests, islands, and deserts.

pages.text: The origin of the program dates back to the mid-20th century. In 1954, Egypt planned to build the Aswan High Dam, which threatened to inundate a large stretch of the Nile valley containing ancient treasures. Consequently, the governments of Egypt and Sudan requested UNESCO's assistance in 1959 to rescue the endangered monuments.
